activity: to interpret a blood pressure reading and explain how diet and exercise change it
story:
The cuff hissed and tightened around his grandfather's arm, and Olivier counted his own heartbeats along with the little bouncing line. They were in the bathroom because that was the only room with a stool, a bright mirror light, and a door his grandmother would not open without knocking, and because after his grandfather's last checkup she had declared that blood pressure was to be discussed in private, the way money used to be. The machine beeped and printed its numbers onto the small screen: 118 over 76.

"What does that mean," his grandfather asked, working his sleeve back down over the mark the cuff had left.

Olivier had the clinic printout folded into his back pocket, and he took it out now and flattened it against his knee. He had been studying it for three days, since the nurse had slid it across the counter and he had caught the numbers before anyone covered them with talk. At first he had only wondered whether 118 over 76 counted as good, and the wondering had catalyzed something that felt unaccountably like ambition. He was starting a nursing assistant course in the fall, six weeks away, and this was the first thing he had tried to learn on his own before anyone assigned it. The pamphlet he had dug out of the recycling bin said the guideline came from the American College of Cardiology and the American Heart Association in 2017, and he had read that sentence so many times it had worn smooth.

"So," he said, hearing his own voice go careful, the way it did when he did not want to get something wrong out loud. "Under the 2017 guideline, normal is below 120 systolic and below 80 diastolic. Both numbers." He touched the printout where the columns of figures ran. "So 118 and 76, that's normal."

His grandfather looked at the ceiling, the way he looked at anything that required him to absorb a number. "Normal," he repeated. Not a question, exactly, but not agreement either. "Last spring Dr. Patel's machine said 130-something and nobody called it normal."

"I know." Olivier turned the page. "I don't know what it was last spring. I wasn't there." This was the part he had rehearsed least, the honest part, and it came out more bluntly than he intended. He had imagined this conversation going smoother, with himself confident at the mirror-lit stool like a person who belonged in scrubs. Instead he was sitting on the edge of the tub holding a wrinkled pamphlet, and the gap between what he knew and what he didn't kept opening under him.

The detente between his grandmother and his grandfather over the subject had been running since spring, his grandmother quietly removing the salt shaker, his grandfather quietly fetching a second one from the garage. Olivier had stayed out of it the way you stay out of a border dispute with no maps. But the pamphlet had a page about food and walking, plain sentences, and he had read them enough to say them in his own words. "It says walking, like every day, regular walking, brings it down over time. And the salt thing, that's real, that's not just Grandma being Grandma." He paused. "The diet part, the exercise part. That's why she's doing it. She read the same pamphlet, I think."

His grandfather's mouth did something that wanted to be a complaint and settled into something else. "She hid the good soy sauce."

"Because of the sodium, probably." Olivier said it gently, and then, because the honesty was already loose in the room, he added, "I can't tell you how much it brings it down. The pamphlet doesn't say exactly, and I don't want to make up a number." He held up the printout. "I know what normal is. I know which side of it you're on today. The rest of it, the how much, I'd be guessing."

They sat with that for a moment, the exhaust fan humming, the mirror holding both of their faces at slightly flattering angles. His grandfather extended his arm again, cuff and all, and tapped the machine's start button with one thick finger. It whirred and squeezed, and the number that came up was 117 over 74, and his grandfather made a small sound, almost effusive for him, a whole celebration compressed into a single syllable of breath.

"Walk with me tomorrow," his grandfather said. "Around the reservoir. Not fast."

"Okay," Olivier said. "I'll bring the cuff."

"Leave the cuff," his grandfather said, standing up, pressing his sleeve flat. "Bring the soy sauce question to your grandmother. Let her win it."

Olivier folded the printout along its old creases and followed him out, switching off the mirror light behind them.

activity: to compute the integral of a function to find the area under a curve
story:
The paper had gone soft where Mya's thumb held it, a warm crescent of sweat at the corner of the page. She had sequestered herself in her grandmother's back bedroom with the ceiling fan clicking overhead, a bowl of pistachios at her elbow, and a worksheet from the tutoring centre downtown where she volunteered on Saturdays. The problem was simple enough to be humiliating: integrate x squared, then x, then x to the negative one, all from one to three.

The first two folded themselves flat under the power rule. Raise the exponent, divide by the new one, evaluate at the bounds. She wrote the answers in her small back-slanted hand and underlined them, feeling the particular pleasure of a machine working as designed.

Then the third one stopped her. Raising the exponent of x to the negative one gave x to the zero, and dividing by zero meant the whole expression came apart in her hands. She sat back. Outside, her grandmother was arguing with the garden hose, and through the window screen came the smell of wet dirt and the hiss of water against concrete.

"It's broken," Mya called through the screen, when her grandmother came up the back steps with mud to her ankles.

"What's broken?"

"The rule. The rule I learned. It eats itself on this one."

Her grandmother dried her hands on her shorts and looked at the page for a long moment, the way she looked at a hand of cards. "When I was your age," she said, "I failed an exam in exactly this spot."

Mya had heard pieces of this before but never the whole shape of it: her grandmother at seventeen, sent to live with an aunt for a summer, supposedly to help with the cousins, really because there wasn't enough money for the school she'd tested into. She'd sequestered herself in the aunt's attic with a borrowed textbook, doing problems by lamplight while the house slept, telling no one. Mya had always pictured the attic as a kind of probity, a sullen devotion to something nobody was going to reward. When the exam came, she'd gotten everything except one question, and the one question was this one.

"You failed it," Mya said now, "and then what?"

"Then I found out the answer and never forgot it." Her grandmother tapped the problem with one muddy finger. "Some gaps are doors. This one has a name attached. It's the natural logarithm of the absolute value of x."

"That's the antiderivative? For this one specifically?"

"That's it. It fills the one gap the power rule leaves. Everything else, your rule handles. This one thing, the logarithm."

Mya wrote it down slowly, the unfamiliar letters like a signature she was forging. Then she evaluated it at her bounds, three and one, and the logarithm of three appeared at the end of her work like a coin surfacing in shallow water. Not a fraction, not a tidy rational number. An irrational one, going on past the edge of what her calculator would show her.

"Why does it work?" she asked. "Why that, of all things?"

Her grandmother shrugged, which startled Mya more than any answer would have. "I could never tell you why. I know that it does, and I know where the rule ends. The why, I decided, could wait for somebody with more time than I had." She picked up the empty pistachio bowl and carried it toward the kitchen, and Mya sat with the fan clicking and the hose still dripping outside.

She tried the next problem on the sheet, x to the negative two, and the power rule took it cleanly, no gap, no door. So the machine still worked everywhere except that single point, and she'd walked right into it the first day. She thought of the attic, of the lamplight, of the one question her grandmother missed, and understood that knowing where a rule ends was itself a kind of knowledge, maybe the older kind. What she couldn't tell was whether the why mattered more than the that, whether her grandmother had been wise or just tired, and she held both of those in her head at once without choosing, the way she held the pistachio shell, turning it over.

She copied the problem into her notebook twice more, until the letters stopped looking forged. Then she took the page to the kitchen, where her grandmother was running water over the bowl, and laid it on the counter beside the sink.

"That one," Mya said, pointing. "Ask me tomorrow."

activity: to use a geographic information system to overlay flood risk and housing on a city map
story:
The departures board at gate C14 flickered from DELAYED to CANCELLED, and Camille opened her laptop on her knees because there was nothing else to do. Her flight to Providence, where she was supposed to start college orientation in nineteen hours, was not flying anywhere. Around her, a peevish man in a golf shirt argued with a gate agent about vouchers, and a family spread peanut butter sandwiches across three seats. Camille had a scholarship weekend assignment due by midnight: map flood risk against housing for a city she had never visited, Wilmington, Delaware, using the GIS program she had opened for the first time that morning in her mother's kitchen.

She had the two files on her desktop. One was a flood zone layer, a pale blue shape along the Christina River. The other was a housing layer, a scatter of small polygons, each one a parcel. Her instructions said to show which homes sat inside the flood zone, and she had assumed the hard part would be finding the data. It had taken her forty minutes on the county's website and a signed affidavit from her mother, scanned and uploaded, to get the parcel file released for student use. Then she had dragged both layers onto the map and felt a small surge of accomplishment, because there they were, the blue shape and the hundreds of tiny parcels, all together on one screen.

She spent a while making it pretty. She changed the parcels to a warm orange. Then she reread the assignment and stopped. It did not ask for homes and flood zones side by side. It asked for homes at risk. On her map, every house in the city was still visible, the ones on the river and the ones three miles inland, and she could not tell from looking which fell inside the blue.

Across from her, a girl about her own age sat cross-legged on the carpet with a battered paperback, a duffel beside her, clearly also stranded. Camille hesitated, then leaned over. "Are you also stuck on the Richmond flight?" The girl looked up. "Raleigh. Same storm, I think." Her name was Priya, and she was starting a geography program in the fall, which Camille learned because Priya asked what she was working on and Camille turned the laptop toward her.

"Those are just stacked," Priya said. "Both layers, everything showing. You need an overlay, a specific one." She scooted over, set the paperback down, and pointed at the toolbar without touching the trackpad. "Intersect. An intersect overlay keeps only the areas that appear in both input layers." Camille found the tool in a dropdown menu, a small icon of two overlapping rectangles. She selected the housing layer, then the flood zone, and clicked.

The map redrew itself. The orange parcels vanished from the inland neighborhoods, from the whole north side of the city, until what remained was a narrow band of shapes along the river, inside the blue, and nothing else. A few dozen parcels. She counted them street by street, then found the tool that gave her the exact number, and wrote it in her notes. Intersecting housing with the flood zone had shown her just the homes inside the zone, which was the assignment, which she had not known how to ask the software to do until two minutes ago.

They worked through the rest together, more or less. Priya showed her how to shade the remaining parcels by the year they were built, and the older ones clustered closest to the water. Camille exported the map as a PDF and started the write-up, and it was here that she slowed down. The prompt asked what the map could and could not tell a city planner. She typed that the intersect was honest about geography but quiet about people, that it said nothing about who lived in those old houses or whether they could leave, and that a planner would have to operationalize fairness some other way, with data the map did not hold. She sat with that sentence for a while, unsure whether it was insight or excuse, and left it in.

Priya read over her shoulder while pretending not to. "You could also run it the other way," she said. "Flood zone first, then housing, and clip to the parcels instead. Same idea, different question." Camille looked at the two rectangles in the toolbar again and understood that she did not yet know what the difference was, or whether it mattered, and that she would find out in a classroom in Providence, or would not. The gate agent announced rebooking at counter four. Priya stood, shouldered her duffel, and pointed at the screen. "Good luck with orientation." Camille saved the file twice, closed the laptop, and got in line.

activity: to lead a holiday meal ceremony from start to finish for the whole family
story:
Luca had told his grandmother he could do it himself, the whole Seder, from the candles to the last cup, and now that the family was actually seated in her crowded dining room he understood that telling and doing were different animals. His uncle Marty had already begun rearranging the Seder plate without asking, sliding the shank bone toward the parsley as though the arrangement were a matter of taste rather than law. Luca put it back.

"You know your grandfather never touched the plate once it was set," his grandmother said from the head of the table. She said it lightly, but Luca heard the measurement underneath. She had wanted him to lead this year because his father was in Barcelona with the new wife, and Luca had agreed partly out of duty and partly, he could admit now, because he wanted to be the one at the head of the table for once. He had never said that to anyone. He had barely said it to himself.

He had learned the hard way that the timing mattered more than he'd assumed. Two weeks ago he had called the community hall to reserve the room for the family Seder, thinking a bigger space would be kinder than his grandmother's cramped dining room, and he had asked for Friday evening because Friday was the date on his phone's calendar, the fifteenth, and the fifteenth was the day the holiday was listed. The hall manager, a patient woman named Rosa, had said, "You want Thursday evening, honey. The evening that starts the holiday, not the evening that ends it. In Judaism, a day begins at sundown." Luca had sat there holding the phone, feeling stupid in the specific way of someone who has been Jewish for seventeen years and never once noticed how the clock worked. He had gotten the evening right. He had almost gotten it wrong. He still didn't fully trust himself on it, which was why he had checked the sunset time twice and arrived at his grandmother's at five, though dinner wasn't until seven.

Now, at the table, his little cousins were already begging for the afikomen hunt to start early, and Marty was telling a story about a business partner he called "an absolute sycophant, the man agrees with everything the client says," and Luca realized he had lost the room. He tapped his glass. Nothing. He tapped it again.

"Luca, sweetheart," said his great-aut Rona, who was ninety-one and had buried two husbands, "just start. Nobody's waiting for permission."

He started. The candle blessing came out lower than he'd practiced it, almost mumbled, but the candles were lit and the room dimmed and then brightened as his grandmother turned on the overheads. When he poured the first cup, Marty reached for the wine immediately and Luca said, "We bless first," and, to his surprise, Marty put the glass down and said, "Right, right," and the table waited. The waiting was the strange part. Luca had spent his whole life at this table being the one who waited.

Between the karpas and the matzah, his cousin Dara, fourteen and newly argumentative, asked why they were doing all this before eating, and Luca began to explain and then stopped, because the honest answer was that he had two ideas in his head that didn't sit together. One was his grandfather's way, learned from watching the man for years: everything in order, no shortcuts, the ceremony as a wall you built carefully so that it would hold. The other was Rona's way, which Luca had absorbed over even more years of dinners: the order was a frame, and what mattered was the argument inside it, the questions, the story told badly and retold. His grandfather had led like a judge. Rona told jokes during the plagues. Luca had spent a month trying to decide which of them he was, and standing there with the Haggadah open he understood he was not going to decide tonight, and that leading might mean holding both and being unsure out loud.

"I don't actually know if we're doing this the way Zayde did," he said. "I think I've mixed some things up."

His grandmother set down her fork. For a moment the room held its breath, and Luca thought he had wrecked it.

"Good," Rona said. "He mixed things up too. He'd deny it, but the man made up half the tunes."

The Seder went on. Luca read the Four Questions with Dara stumbling beside him, then managed the Ten Plagues with the cousins flicking grape juice at each plague, which Rona had started and Luca, after one breath of hesitation, allowed. During the meal he caught himself inventing a memory, a smooth false recollection of his grandfather teaching him the tune for Dayenu, and he stopped mid-verse because it hadn't happened that way; his grandfather had mostly ignored him at Seders, and it was Rona who had sung. He had been rewriting the man all evening, softening him into a teacher. He wondered what else he'd rewritten.

At the end, after the fourth cup, the cousins found the afikomen behind the radiator, and Luca paid the ransom, and his grandmother took his hand across the table before he could begin the closing. Outside the window the sky had gone fully dark hours ago, which meant, he thought, that they were deep inside the holiday now rather than at its edge, that the whole evening had been the beginning of something rather than the end of a preparation.

"Next year," his grandmother said, "you'll do it in the hall. Rosa is holding Thursday evening for you."

"Thursday," Luca said.

activity: to pass a driving test by practising parallel parking and merging on the highway
story:
Kate's father had backed the family car between two wheelbarrows in the garage, leaving a space barely longer than the car itself, and now he stood by the door with his arms crossed while she sat behind the wheel doing nothing. "You can't just look at it," he said. She inched forward, reversed, and clipped a wheelbarrow with the rear bumper on the first attempt and the second. On the third she stopped halfway through and put the handbrake on so hard it sounded like a protest.

"I've been practising bay parking for two months," she said. "Bay parking is easy. You drive into a car park and slot in. This is different." Her father shrugged. "The examiner might not ask for bays at all." He said it casually, the way he said most things, and Kate felt something cold move through her, because she had spent every Sunday since February in the Tesco car park reversing into painted white lines, and she had never once asked what else the test could contain.

That night she lay on her bed with her phone above her face and typed the question into the search bar. She read the answer twice, then sat up. On the practical driving test in Great Britain, parallel parking at the side of the road was one of the reversing manoeuvres the examiner may ask a candidate to do. It wasn't a rumour or a worst-case scenario. It was one of the options, written plainly, and the examiner could choose it. She had been preparing for a question that might not be asked while ignoring a question that very likely would be.

She texted her friend Dev, who had passed her test in March. "Did you get bay parking or parallel on yours?" Dev replied a minute later: "Parallel. On a road with a bus behind me. The bus driver did not love me that day." Then: "Also why are you messaging me at 11pm about parking, is this what your life has become, where is the hedonism I was promised, where are our wild teenage years." Kate laughed into her pillow and typed back that her wild teenage years were currently incapacitated by two wheelbarrows, and that she would let them out again on Thursday, after the test.

Thursday was four days away. The next morning she moved the operation to the road outside the house, where her father stood in for the car in front and the neighbour's actual car stood in for the car behind, its owner having agreed on the condition that Kate touch nothing but kerb. Her first attempts were lugubrious affairs, long slow reverses with the car drifting at an angle that suggested surrender, and the neighbour watched from his window with what Kate chose to interpret as sympathy.

"Find your reference point," her father said, which was the most instruction he ever gave. She learned to line the back of the parked car up with her rear passenger window, turn full lock, watch the kerb rise in the wing mirror, straighten, turn the other way. It began to feel less like geometry and more like a sentence she could say fluently. What she could not reconcile was the two different theories of driving she seemed to hold at once. In the car park she had learned precision, the belief that a space could be measured and taken. On the road, with the bus in Dev's story sitting on her bumper, precision felt like a luxury; the real skill was decision, choosing a gap and committing to it while the world leaned on its horn.

On Wednesday her father took her onto the ring road to practise merging, which was the other half of what she feared. The slip road was short and the traffic was thick and she stopped at the dashed line instead of joining, which was the wrong thing, and a van behind her made its feelings known. "You have to arrive already moving," her father said. They went around again. The second time she looked over her shoulder, matched her speed to a gap between a lorry and a hatchback, and slid into it, and for six seconds the two theories were the same theory: measure the space, but do not stop moving while you measured it.

On the morning of the test she sat in the test centre car park while the examiner, a small brisk woman with a clipboard, wrote something down and then looked up. "Right. We'll go out, and at some point I'll ask you to do one of the reversing manoeuvres." Kate's hands were steady on the wheel. She did not know which one it would be, and she was honest with herself about that; the not knowing would sit beside her the whole way round, and she would drive with it there. The examiner clipped in her seatbelt. "Follow the road ahead, please."

activity: to build a class in Java with private fields and getter methods and test it
story:
Charlotte had claimed the corner computer by the large-print westerns because it was the only terminal with a working semicolon key, and she needed semicolons the way other people needed oxygen. Her summer assignment, emailed in June by a professor she had not yet met, was to build a class called Book with private fields and getter methods, then test it. She had never written a line of Java before Tuesday.

The library smelled of carpet glue and old paper. Three tables away, a boy she recognized from AP Computer Science, Dev, was failing to look busy over a laptop covered in dinosaur stickers. She had come here partly because of him, though she hadn't admitted that to herself yet, and partly because her apartment had no internet and her stepfather had opinions about lazy girls playing on computers all day.

She typed the class in twenty minutes. Fields for title and pages, both private, then methods named getTitle and getPages that handed the values back. She wrote a small test class, BookTest, and in it she tried to print the pages directly, because that was how her brain wanted the world to work. She hit compile.

The compiler refused. It underlined her line in red and said the field was private. She read the message three times, then a fourth, as if the words might rearrange themselves. Something in her chest went tight and visceral, the same drop she felt when a teacher paused beside her desk too long.

"Dev," she called, keeping her voice low. "Does yours compile?"

He came over and read her screen. "There. You're touching pages from outside the class."

"I'm printing it. That's not touching."

"It is to Java." He pulled a chair around, which she noted, and filed away, and did not comment on. "A field marked private can be read or changed only by code inside the same class. You're in BookTest. BookTest is not Book."

"So I have to use the getter."

"Or make the field public, but Professor Okafor will fail you for that. It's the whole point of the assignment."

She deleted her line and called getPages instead, and the compiler went quiet and green, and a number she had asked for appeared on the screen. She sat back. It had refused her, and then, when she asked correctly, it had given her exactly what she wanted, and she could not decide if that was a courtesy or a trap.

For an hour they worked side by side, trading the keyboard. She learned to make a setter that refused negative page counts, throwing an exception with a message she got to write herself, and she spent a shameless amount of time on the wording of that message. At four o'clock Dev closed his laptop and stood, and she asked the question she had been holding all afternoon.

"Why did you follow me here? You don't come to this library."

He looked at the westerns instead of at her. "Because my scholarship got rescinded in May. My SAT scores were flagged. I retake them in August and if I don't get the money back, I don't go anywhere in the fall." He shrugged with one shoulder. "You're the only person I know who actually finishes things. I figured some of it would amortize. The discipline, I mean. Spread out over me."

She thought about culpability, hers or the testing company's or nobody's, and how he had sat three tables away for two days being casual while the whole summer balanced on one morning in August. She had wanted him to follow her, she could admit that now, but she had wanted it to be about her.

"I finish things," she said, "because my stepfather says I won't."

"Then finish this." He slid a blank piece of paper across the table. "Write your Book class on it. By hand. No compiler to catch you. If you can do it on paper, you actually know it, and I need to know if this method works before I waste August on it."

She picked up her pen. The paper was thin enough that the wood of the table showed through, and she could hear the copier running somewhere near the front desk, and the air conditioning clicking on.

"Title first," she said, and wrote the word private.

activity: to read a short news article in a new language and summarise it aloud
story:
The folding table at the edge of the festival had a hand-painted banner that said Read the News, Win a Pastel, and beneath it a girl about Amy's age sat guarding a stack of clipped articles like a dragon with a library card. Amy had walked past the table twice. Her grandmother had spoken Portuguese around the house her whole childhood, half-understood, like weather through a wall, and this fall she would start college three hours from anyone who could correct her. The banner seemed to be addressed to exactly that fear. On her third pass she stopped.

"Rules," said the girl, whose name tag read Marisa. "You pick a short article. You read it, no dictionary, no phone. Then you tell me what it says, out loud, in Portuguese. If I understand you, you get the pastel. If I don't, you get the pastel anyway, but you have to listen to me complain about your grammar first."

"Generous," Amy said, and drew a clipping from the stack.

Before she sat down, the boy at the next chair leaned over. His name was Tomas, he said, he'd been in the country for four months, and he was staring at a local newspaper's front page with an expression of personal betrayal. "This headline," he said, tapping it. "Mayor Quits After Bridge Closed. Where is the grammar? Where are the little words? It says the bridge is closed now, but the article says it closed in March. It quits grammar, this newspaper."

Amy looked at the headline, then at the article, and something rearranged itself in her head with an almost audible click. "It's not broken," she said slowly. "It's compressed. English headlines drop the small words like 'the,' and they use present tense for past events. It's a style. I think it's even called headlinese." She pointed. "Quits means quit. Closed means closed. Somebody decided small words were too expensive."

"Somebody decided grammar was too expensive," Tomas said, but he was grinning now, copying the headline into a notebook with evident delight. "It has its own ontology, this headline language. Its own way of existing. Like a tiny separate universe where nothing is ever past tense and nothing has a the."

"Four months in and you're already philosophizing in English," Amy said. "That's either very fast or very alarming."

He shrugged. "My uncle says my brain has not yet ossified. Everything is still soft. I can learn anything, including apparently a language with no verbs' endings."

Amy turned back to her article, a short piece about a city council vote on a new park, and read it twice through. Her Portuguese came up out of that childhood weather, unreliable and unsummonable. When she opened her mouth for Marisa, nerves did to her exactly what the newspaper had done: she dropped every small word she could, hoping the load would fit in fewer pieces. "Conselho... aprova... parque... sábado." She stopped, hearing herself, and laughed. "I just gave you a headline. That's all that was."

Marisa tilted her head, considering. "I understood it. But you sound like you're being billed by the word. The little words are auxiliary to nothing if you leave them out; they're the road the sentence walks on. Try again. Tell me the story."

Amy took a breath and began again, slower, letting the articles and prepositions back in, letting Saturday be past, letting the council have voted and the mayor have argued and the vote have been close. Her sentences limped and one verb came out in a tense that made Marisa wince on her behalf, but the story arrived: the park, the fight over the trees, the six-to-five vote. When she finished, Marisa slid the pastel across the table without a word of complaint, which Amy chose to take as a passing grade.

Then Marisa flipped the clipping over, and on the back, in blue pen, was another article, cut from a different paper entirely. The headline read: Girl Wins Pastry at Festival Booth. "I wrote that one myself this morning," Marisa said. "For the next person. You're famous, in headlinese. Present tense, no small words, eternal glory." Amy looked at the words, at the greasy paper bag in her hand, at Tomas copying the style into his notebook for future use, and decided she would take the pastel and leave the immortality. She split it with Tomas anyway, right down the middle, the crumbs falling on both their articles like confetti.

activity: to build a class in Java with private fields and getter methods and test it
story:
Zoe had never written a class before, and Priya's basement smelled like dust and the electric breath of an old space heater, which seemed right for a place where something moribund might be brought back to life. Her laptop was open on the ping-pong table, the cursor blinking in an empty file called Student.java. Priya sat cross-legged on the couch behind her, eating dry cereal out of the box and watching a video about white blood cells for her nursing program, occasionally saying things like "so the antigen is the thing the antibody recognizes," which Zoe filed away as a fact from a country she did not live in.

"Okay," Zoe said. "Fields first. Name, ID, GPA."

"Private," Priya said without looking up. "You told me that part twice already. You pontificate when you're nervous, you know that?"

"I don't pontificate, I recap." But she typed private String name; private int id; private double gpa; and then sat there. The fields sat there too, hidden, like the inside of a cell she couldn't see through. That was the point, apparently. That was what she'd signed up for when she'd registered for the intro course and then panicked about being behind everyone who'd coded since middle school.

The problem was concrete: her homework required a class whose data nobody outside could touch directly, with getter methods to read the fields, and a test class proving it all worked. The want was less concrete and larger, which was that in nine days she would be a college student, and she did not intend to be the one in the lecture hall raising her hand to ask what everyone else already knew. So she was here, in a basement, a week early, teaching herself.

She wrote getName() and getId() and getGpa(), each one a line returning its hidden value, and it struck her as strange, this whole ceremony. Why lock the door and then hand out a key to anyone who knocks? She asked Priya, who paused her video.

"Isn't that like, the immune thing? Nothing gets in except through the receptor?"

"Sort of not at all," Priya said, "but keep going."

Zoe built the test class. Student s = new Student(); and then she tried s.name = "Zoe"; and the compiler refused her in red, underlining the trespass, and she felt an actual jolt of something like delight. The refusal was the proof. She changed it to s = new Student with a constructor she wrote herself, then System.out.println(s.getName()); and ran it, and the name printed in the console, clean and black on white, arriving through the proper channel. She put both hands above her head like she'd scored a goal, and Priya clapped twice, deadpan, a piece of cereal in one hand.

"Who even made this language?" Priya asked, leaning over to look. "It feels old."

"It is old, I think." Zoe opened a new tab and typed the question, and the answer came back fast: Java had been released by Sun Microsystems in 1995, and its lead designer was a man named James Gosling. Nineteen ninety-five. She did the math twice, because it didn't seem possible. The language was older than both of them, older than the basement laptop, older than half the furniture down here, and it had been running the whole time while she was being born and learning to walk and failing algebra, still going, still the thing her college expected her to know.

"It's older than us," she said. "Java's older than us. Some guy named James Gosling designed it at Sun Microsystems before we existed."

"Huh," Priya said. "So it works and it's old. Like Latin, but with jobs."

Zoe looked at her test output again, the getter returning exactly what the constructor had stored, the private field safe behind its methods, and she tried to hold two thoughts at once. One was that this was elegant, that a language built before she was born had already solved the problem of trust, of deciding who gets access, and all she had to do was learn its rules. The other was that the rules were the kind you couldn't argue with, that the compiler's red underline didn't care about her reasons, and she wasn't sure yet whether that felt like safety or like a door with only one side. Maybe both. Maybe that was the actual answer and she'd find out in nine days, or in four years, or never.

"Run it again," Priya said, setting down the cereal box and scooting over, her antigen video forgotten. "I want to watch it refuse you one more time."
